strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-documented problem: instability of circuit discovery under changes to the concept dataset (citing Meloux et al. 2025, Miller et al. 2024, Friedman et al. 2024). Framing dataset-to-circuit stability as a certification problem is a genuinely novel angle for mechanistic interpretability.

The framework is algorithm-agnostic and simple: run the base discovery algorithm on random dataset deletions, aggregate per-vertex votes, and abstain when no robust decision is possible. This makes it applicable to a range of base methods without internal access.

The proof of Theorem 3.1 (App. A) is correct and clearly written: it is a careful instantiation of RS-Del (Huang et al., 2023) with per-component abstention (Fischer et al., 2021), including a proper union-bound treatment for simultaneous per-vertex guarantees.

The empirical evaluation is broad for a first paper in this direction: ResNet-50/101 on ImageNet, four OOD benchmarks (OOD-CV, ImageNet-A/O/C), three scoring functions, sufficiency and compactness curves (Fig. 3), class-specificity analysis (App. C), and a structural stability (IoU) analysis (Fig. 4) that tests an additional prediction of the mechanism.
Honest limitations section discussing compute overhead, the radius/deletion-rate trade-off, single layer-wise sparsity budget, and restriction to CNNs.
weaknesses: The certified radius is extremely weak in practice: with pdel=0.6 and τ=0.95 the experiments certify only r=1 dataset edit. Appendix B even states the goal of 'a meaningful certified radius (e.g., r ≥ 5 edits)', but this is never achieved in the main results. The headline claim of 'provable stability guarantees' is therefore much narrower than the framing suggests — stability to a single insertion/deletion/substitution.

The theoretical contribution is modest: Theorem 3.1 is essentially a corollary of RS-Del applied to a binary per-vertex classifier, combined with the known segmentation-style abstention rule. The novelty is in the application, not the analysis.

A key confound is not ablated: the certified circuit is essentially a majority-vote/top-agreement ensemble over subsampled datasets with abstention. The paper compares only to the raw single-run top-K baseline. Baselines such as (i) ensembling/majority-vote without certification, (ii) thresholding inclusion frequency without the τ-margin, or (iii) simply using a smaller K, are needed to isolate whether the certification machinery (rather than averaging over resamples) drives the OOD and compactness gains.

The certified property concerns the smoothed algorithm A˜τ, which the authors themselves construct; invariance of a self-constructed smoothed rule is close to by-construction. The link between certified stability under r=1 edit and OOD generalization is empirical, not guaranteed, yet the abstract/conclusion blur this distinction.

Some evaluation choices appear favorable to the method: structural stability in Fig. 4 is evaluated 'at the K that maximizes the certified–baseline cACC gap', a selection criterion biased toward the proposed method; headline gains are reported as relative percentages (e.g., '91% higher accuracy' from 37% vs 19% absolute; '104% ΔcACC' from small absolute bases) without confidence intervals or significance tests.

Threat model motivation is loose: edit distance is defined over an arbitrarily ordered sequence of images, while concept datasets are unordered sets; the certificate's meaning under this metric deserves more scrutiny, and ImageNet class folders (~1300 images) may make a 1-edit radius even less meaningful.

Evaluation is restricted to channel-level circuits in CNNs (ResNet-50/101); the most prominent modern circuit discovery work is on transformers/LLMs, and no evidence is given that the approach transfers. Code is not yet available ('will be released soon'), limiting reproducibility of the reported numbers.

Results where circuit-only accuracy (96%) far exceeds the full model (81%) on ImageNet indicate the pruning removes 'competing' features; the paper would benefit from more careful discussion of whether such circuits remain faithful mechanistic explanations rather than simply discriminative subnetworks.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and timely problem: discovered circuits are brittle under dataset variation, and it is the first (to my knowledge) to attach a formal, dataset-level edit-distance certificate to circuit component decisions rather than diagnosing instability only (Meloux et al. 2025; Miller et al. 2024).

The framework is algorithm-agnostic in principle: the smoothing wrapper (RS-Del + per-component abstention, combining Huang et al. 2023 with Fischer et al. 2021) applies to any dataset-to-mask discovery rule, and the proof in App. A is correct as a direct instantiation of RS-Del with binary outputs.

The evaluation is broad for a first work: three scoring functions, two ResNets, four OOD benchmarks (OOD-CV, ImageNet-A, ImageNet-O, ImageNet-C), cACC-vs-K sweeps, class-specificity (oACC) analysis in the appendix, and a structural-stability (IoU) experiment that goes beyond accuracy numbers.
The abstention mechanism as 'adaptive sparsity' is a nice practical byproduct, and the limitations section is reasonably honest about compute cost, small datasets, and CNN-only scope.
weaknesses: The certified radius is the central selling point, yet the experiments certify only r = 1 (pdle=0.6, tau=0.95, Sec. 4): stability under a single dataset edit. This makes the headline claim of 'provable stability guarantees' and 'formal ground for circuit discovery' very thin in practice. Worse, App. B states the goal is a 'meaningful certified radius (e.g., r >= 5 edits),' directly contradicting the main text. The abstract/intro rhetoric (r=5 covering 'an exponentially large family of datasets') oversells what is actually certified.

There is a gap between what is certified and what is evaluated. The theorem guarantees invariance of the smoothed mapping A_tau under r edits, but the empirical claims (OOD gains up to 91%, IoU stability on shifted data) concern behavior far beyond the certified radius; the paper acknowledges circuits are evaluated 'beyond their certified radius,' so the certificate does very little explanatory work for the headline results.

Empirical results are extraordinary and under-analyzed: class-specific pruned circuits (34% of channels) achieve ~94% cACC on ImageNet-A where the full ResNet-101 attains ~9%. Zeroing channels apparently denoises adversarial data more than the full network, which is a striking claim that needs much deeper analysis (e.g., what features are removed, calibration/confusion analysis) before it can support the mechanistic-interpretability narrative.

Comparisons are confounded by size. Headline gains compare peak cACC at different K (certified 0.34 vs baseline 0.40-0.80). While Fig. 3 shows curves, the certified circuit's size is data-dependent (post-abstention), so a matched-capacity or matched-compute baseline (e.g., simply ensembling top-K over subsamples without certification) is missing; the gains may largely reflect subsample-voting/regularization rather than certification itself.

The base algorithm tested is only a trivial top-K channel scorer (activation/relevance/rank). The 'wraps any black-box discovery algorithm' claim is demonstrated only for fixed top-K rules; no iterative methods (ACDC-style), no transformers, no spurious-feature ablation matching the motivating Fig. 1 anecdote. The title's 'Mechanistic Circuits' is thus broader than what is studied.

Reproducibility is weak: 'Code will be released soon!' with no anonymized code, and several presentation problems undermine trust in the numbers (garbled Table 2, the Figure 1 caption '62% over baseline' vs. Table 1's 12% for ImageNet relevance, inconsistent percentage claims between abstract, Sec. 5, and tables).

Threat-model realism is under-argued: edit distance over an arbitrarily ordered dataset of images treats swapping one photograph for another as one edit, but the certificate says nothing about the semantic equivalence of the swapped example, which is exactly the failure mode the paper motivates (spurious cues). The certificate is thus about decision stability under dataset resampling, not about the circuit 'capturing the concept' as the abstract implies.

Only 100 classes, a single fixed pdel/tau operating point, and a single shared K across layers; no sensitivity analysis of the results to these choices in the main text, despite the certificate depending critically on them.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-documented and important problem: the fragility of discovered mechanistic circuits to the choice of concept dataset (Meloux et al. 2025; Miller et al. 2024; Friedman et al. 2024). Framing circuit discovery as a dataset-level mapping and asking for certified invariance is a natural and novel connection between certified robustness and mechanistic interpretability.

The method is algorithm-agnostic and technically sound as far as presented: Theorem 3.1 is a correct and cleanly written application of RS-Del (Huang et al., 2023) to a per-vertex binary classifier, combined with per-component abstention in the style of certified segmentation (Fischer et al., 2021). The appendix proof is complete, including the union-bound treatment for simultaneous per-vertex guarantees.

The empirical evaluation is broad: two architectures (ResNet-50/101), three scoring functions, and four OOD benchmarks, with complementary metrics (sufficiency cACC, compactness K, class specificity oACC, and structural stability via IoU). The three-stage cACC-vs-K analysis is insightful, and the paper reports that certified circuits become both smaller and more class-specific (oACC drops to ~1%).

The limitations and discussion sections are honest and specific: they disclose the linear runtime scaling, the pdel/radius trade-off, the layer-wise budget simplification, and the restriction to CNNs, and they carefully position the work against the concurrent Anonymous (2026) verification-based approach. The impact statement appropriately cautions against over-reading certificates.
weaknesses: The certified radius actually achieved is r=1 (pdel=0.6, τ=0.95), meaning the certificate only guarantees invariance under a single example insertion/deletion/substitution. This is a very weak guarantee, in tension with the abstract's framing ('provable stability guarantees... bounded edit-distance perturbations' and App. B's stated goal of r ≥ 5). Since radius grows only as pdel → 1, which starves the base algorithm, the framework appears fundamentally limited to radii of 1–2 for realistic concept datasets. This gap between the marketed guarantee and the delivered certificate is the paper's most significant weakness and is not confronted head-on.

The certificate covers stability of the smoothed pipeline's own decisions under tiny dataset edits; it says nothing about the OOD generalization gains that headline the paper. Certified radius 1 does not connect to transfer to ImageNet-A/OOD-CV, yet the abstract and introduction imply stability is what underpins OOD robustness. The logical link is asserted ('stability is a prerequisite for OOD generalization') but not demonstrated.

A decisive missing baseline: an uncertified aggregation variant (e.g., majority vote over the same n subsamples without abstention, or pruning to matched size via consensus scores). Without it, the experiments cannot isolate whether the gains come from certified abstention specifically or merely from ensembling/subsampling and selecting a smaller circuit. Given that abstention-induced size reduction is the proposed mechanism, this control is essential.

All 'peak cACC' results are reported at the K maximizing accuracy (and, in Fig. 4, at the K maximizing the certified–baseline gap), i.e., selected post hoc per condition. This oracle-style selection can inflate both methods' numbers, and the fairness of the certified-vs-baseline comparison at these selected operating points is unclear.

Baseline diversity is thin: only top-K channel selection with three scoring functions. No comparison to other instability-mitigation heuristics or to the stronger circuit discovery methods discussed in related work; all conclusions rest on one discovery paradigm.
No code is available ('Code will be released soon!'), which, combined with the many moving parts (pdel, τ, n, α, scoring functions, per-dataset K selection), limits reproducibility at review time.

Relative-improvement framing ('up to 91% higher accuracy') is driven by very low baseline points (e.g., 19% → 37% on ImageNet-A with Activation scoring); absolute gains and the inconsistent behavior across scoring functions (e.g., Activation: +1% on ImageNet vs. Rank: +76% in Table 1) suggest the method's benefit is sensitive to the base algorithm, which deserves analysis rather than only best-case reporting.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: the paper provides the first framework for certifying dataset-level stability of circuit discovery, directly addressing documented instability issues (Méloux et al. 2025; Miller et al. 2024; Friedman et al. 2024).

Clean, technically sound construction: combining RS-Del deletion smoothing (Huang et al., 2023) with per-component abstention certification (Fischer et al., 2021) is a natural and correct composition; the proof of Theorem 3.1 (App. A) and the Monte Carlo estimation scheme (Alg. 1-2 with FWER control) are careful, including the union-bound treatment over |U| components.

Broad and convincing empirical validation across modalities, architectures, and base algorithms (ResNet-50/101, ViT-B/16, GPT-2 Small; top-K relevance/activation/rank; EAP-IG on IOI/IOI-Hard/Greater-Than), with paired significance tests, uncertainty estimates, and an informative seed-stability analysis (mean IoU 0.973 across 40 seeds).

Good ablations that isolate the contribution: the majority-vote comparison (App. F.5) shows gains beyond ensemble averaging, and the runtime analysis (App. D) demonstrates practicality (~2.4x overhead via score caching).

Honest limitations discussion: acknowledges the r=1 vision setting, the |D| dependence of larger radii, the single layer-wise sparsity budget, and the distinction from concurrent input-perturbation certification work (Hadad et al., 2026).
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: the core guarantee is a direct composition of two existing certification tools (RS-Del + SegCertify); the proof is a straightforward application, so the contribution is primarily an application/systems insight rather than a new certification technique.

The main vision results use a certified radius of only r=1 (a single dataset edit), which is a weak practical guarantee; larger radii (App. F.4) require much larger concept datasets (|D| >= 500-1000), limiting the strength of the certification in typical use.

Hyperparameter selection raises fairness concerns: for language, pdel and tau are 'tuned per task and the best configuration' is reported (Sec. 4, App. B.2), and the tuning criterion is evaluated on the same tasks used for headline results; certified vs. baseline comparisons could thus be partly driven by selection effects.

Some reported numbers are surprising and insufficiently explained: e.g., the baseline circuit achieves 0.60 cACC on ImageNet-A while the full model achieves 0.07 (Table 1); a mechanism for why pruning a 60%-collapsed model to a circuit yields 60% accuracy on natural adversarial examples deserves analysis.

Only GPT-2 Small is evaluated for language, and only 100 ImageNet classes (50 images each) for vision; the paper's own limitations note that extension to larger language models remains open, leaving generalizability claims somewhat modest.

Presentation issues: missing code link in the abstract, typos ('condsider'), several appendix figures (Figs. 13-15) have mangled axes/legend rendering, and the headline 'up to 56% higher accuracy' is a relative gain on a single benchmark that risks overstatement in the abstract.

strengths: Addresses a real, documented problem in mechanistic interpretability (dataset-level instability of discovered circuits, per Méloux et al. 2025, Miller et al. 2024, Friedman et al. 2024) with the first dataset-level certification framework for circuit discovery — a clear and well-motivated gap.

The framework is genuinely algorithm-agnostic and modality-agnostic: it wraps node-level top-K scorers and edge-level EAP-IG across ResNet-50/101, ViT-B/16, and GPT-2 Small, on ID and four OOD benchmarks, which is unusually broad empirical coverage for this area.

The ablations are convincing and pre-empt the obvious objections: the majority-vote baseline at matched compute (App. F.5) isolates the contribution of the τ-threshold from mere ensemble averaging; the seed-stability experiment (App. F.2) and radius-scaling analysis (App. F.4) map out when certification helps; the runtime analysis (App. D) shows the n-sample cost is mitigated by caching (~2.4× overhead).

The proof (App. A) is correct as far as presented: it is a careful instantiation of RS-Del on per-component binary classifiers with a Clopper–Pearson lower bound and Bonferroni/FWER control, and the paper is transparent that the estimator combines SegCertify and RS-Del.

Limitations are discussed honestly (small concept datasets limit radii, single shared sparsity K, unvalidated extension to larger LMs), and the impact statement appropriately cautions against over-interpreting certified explanations.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Theorem 3.1 is a direct composition of existing results — RS-Del (Huang et al., 2023) for edit-distance certification and SegCertify-style per-component abstention (Fischer et al., 2021) — with the 'key observation' (App. C.3) that circuit components can be treated as segmentation pixels. The conceptual move (dataset = sequence, component = pixel) is neat but thin; no new proof techniques or certified-radius theory beyond plugging into RS-Del's Theorem 7.

The certified guarantee actually delivered is weak where the paper's main results are: on vision, the default configuration certifies only r = 1 (a single dataset edit, Table 2), which is a very low bar for the headline claim of 'provable stability' under bounded edits. The paper's justification that larger radii require |Dc| ≥ 500–1000 images per concept (App. F.4) substantially narrows the practical relevance of the guarantee.

The deletion-based smoothing configuration is aggressive and strained: pdel = 0.6 on 50-image vision concept datasets (leaving ~20 images per run) and pdel up to 0.99 for language, with τ and pdel tuned per task/split (Table 2, App. B.2 'report the best configuration'). Selecting hyperparameters to maximize peak cACC per evaluation setting risks overfitting the reported numbers, and the metric is itself noisy (Table 5 shows ±0.09–0.13 spreads on OOD-CV for several conditions).

There is a metric-level concern the paper does not fully resolve: certified circuits exceed even the full model's accuracy (e.g., 0.94 on ImageNet-A where the full model attains 0.07; 0.95 on ImageNet where the model attains 0.78). This indicates the sufficiency metric (zeroing non-circuit channels) behaves as a denoiser, so cACC gains may partly reflect a measurement artifact of channel pruning rather than better 'concept capture'; the paper interprets this favorably without deeper analysis (e.g., comparing against pruning-matched random or mutual-information baselines).

The threat model is somewhat artificial: concept datasets are unordered, yet certificates are defined over an arbitrary fixed ordering with edit distance; the paper asserts permutation invariance of base algorithms, but substitutions in the edit-distance ball are only indirectly covered via RS-Del, and the semantic meaning of 'r edits' (e.g., r = 59 on Greater-Than out of 100 examples) is hard to interpret.

Headline numbers ('up to 56% higher accuracy, up to 80% fewer components') are best-case per-setting values rather than central tendencies; across Table 5, gains under the rank scorer shrink to ↑2–20% with ↓2% compactness, suggesting the effect is sensitive to the base scorer's vote distribution.

Reproducibility details are uneven: code is referenced but the link is empty in the provided manuscript; the mechanism by which the effective certified size K is compared against the baseline (certified K is post-abstention) makes some Table 1 comparisons operating-point-dependent rather than strictly matched.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: dataset-to-circuit instability is a real and recently documented weakness of circuit discovery methods (Méloux et al., 2025; Miller et al., 2024; Friedman et al., 2024), and the paper is the first to offer a formal, dataset-level stability guarantee for discovered circuits.

Algorithm-agnostic design is a genuine practical advantage: the framework wraps any black-box discovery algorithm (top-K scorers in vision, EAP-IG in language) without internals access, and the reduction of component certification to binary segmentation (Fischer et al., 2021) combined with RS-Del deletion smoothing (Huang et al., 2023) is technically sound. The proof of Theorem 3.1 is correct, and the statistical treatment (Clopper–Pearson bounds, Bonferroni FWER control over thousands of components, sample-complexity analysis in App. C.2/Fig. 8) is careful.

Unusually broad empirical validation: three architectures (ResNet-50/101, ViT-B/16), two modalities (ImageNet + four OOD benchmarks; GPT-2 Small on IOI/IOI-Hard/Greater-Than), three base scorers (App. F.1), and multiple supporting analyses — majority-vote ablation isolating the contribution of the threshold τ (Fig. 16), 40-seed stability (IoU > 0.95; Fig. 11), structural-stability re-discovery on shifted data (Fig. 6), radius/|Dc| trade-off sweeps (Figs. 13–15), and a runtime analysis showing caching reduces the n-sample overhead to ~2.4× (Table 4).

Good presentation overall: the pipeline (Fig. 2), the certified-in/abstain/certified-out feature visualization (Fig. 5, 17–19), and per-dataset hyperparameter reporting (Table 2) make the method easy to follow, and the limitations section is candid about overhead, dataset-size constraints, and scope relative to the concurrent verification approach (Hadad et al., 2026).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Theorem 3.1 is a direct composition of RS-Del with SegCertify-style per-component abstention; the proof is a short corollary of Huang et al. (2023) applied to a binary smoothed classifier. The contribution is a well-executed combination and application rather than new certification theory.

The headline guarantee is very weak in the main vision results: at pdel = 0.6, τ = 0.95 the certified radius is r = 1 (Table 2), i.e., stability against a single dataset edit. The larger language radii (r = 42–59) come from pdel = 0.99 on |D| = 100 prompts, meaning the base algorithm runs on sub-datasets of expected size ~1 example — an operating regime whose meaningfulness for EAP-IG deserves more scrutiny than the appendix provides.

Hyperparameter selection risks evaluation bias: τ and pdel are tuned per task/split and 'the configuration with the highest peak cACC' is reported (App. B.2), i.e., selection appears to be done on the evaluated configuration, partly on OOD splits. The baseline does not receive an equivalent tuning budget, so some of the reported gains may be optimistic.

Some empirical claims warrant more scrutiny: the 'up to 56% higher accuracy' on ImageNet-A (certified 0.94 vs. full model 0.07) is a striking result that is explained only qualitatively (suppression of spurious paths); and the ImageNet-O setup is confusingly described, since ImageNet-O by construction contains classes outside the ImageNet-1k label set, yet the paper claims the same 100 ID classes are used for every OOD dataset except OOD-CV (App. B.1).

The guarantee covers only non-abstaining components, so the size of the certified subset depends on the abstention rate, which varies widely across settings (up to 50–75% abstention at larger radii, Fig. 14); the paper does not always report abstention rates alongside the headline accuracy/size numbers, making the strength-vs-coverage trade-off hard to assess in Table 1.

Minor presentation issues: an empty code link in the abstract, typos ('condsider'), and several low-legibility appendix figures; language-task cACC is saturated at 100% on ID for both methods, limiting the information content of those comparisons beyond compactness.
